title: Trump Warns Houthis Are 'Behaving Very Badly' as Saudi Arabia Counts the Cost of Riyadh Strikes
excerpt: Washington weighs how far to back Riyadh after new interceptions, while the kingdom absorbs the economic and reputational damage of a war it did not start.
body:
• President Donald Trump said on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and that he might ask Turkey's President Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi Arabia, according to Reuters.
  • Saudi air defences have intercepted further Houthi attacks since the Riyadh airport strike that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, Bloomberg reported.
  • Riyadh is weighing a large-scale response while counting economic costs: a paralysed capital airport sits at odds with Vision 2030's pitch to investors and visitors.
  • Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia should follow the embassy's stay-indoors advisory and expect continued flight disruption through at least October 17.

The cost to Saudi Arabia of the United States' war on Iran moved to the centre of the Gulf crisis on Tuesday, as President Donald Trump warned that Yemen's Houthi movement was "behaving very badly" and Saudi Arabia intercepted further attacks after the deadly strike on Riyadh's airport. Trump told reporters he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene and support Saudi interests, Reuters reported.

"President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask."

— Donald Trump, US President, via Reuters

New attacks after the airport strike

The Houthis, who have fought Yemen's Saudi-backed government since 2014, have escalated attacks on Red Sea shipping and on Saudi territory since the US-Iran war began eight months ago, according to Reuters. The strike on King Khalid International Airport in recent days killed 13 people, wounded more than 300 and closed the skies over the capital. Bloomberg reported that Saudi Arabia has since intercepted new Houthi attacks as the conflict drags on, and CBS News described the attacks as creating a difficult dilemma for Trump: how far to go in defending a partner without widening the war.

Why Riyadh is exposed

The Washington Post's reporting, reflected across regional coverage, frames Saudi Arabia's problem plainly: it is absorbing the costs of a war it did not start. Le Monde reported that the economic, military and psychological costs are already being felt, and that an attack of this scale, with air traffic paralysed, runs against Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's programme to attract foreign investment and reduce dependence on oil. The same reporting said bin Salman has repeatedly asked Trump to act alongside him against the Houthis, while US support has so far been limited to intelligence. Saudi Arabia has sought defensive backing from France and the United Kingdom and activated a defence pact signed with Pakistan and Turkey.

The Indian stake

Saudi Arabia hosts a large Indian workforce, and the airport attacks have already killed and injured Indian nationals — see our coverage of the embassy advisory after the Riyadh attack. Indian airlines have cancelled Saudi flights as Riyadh's airport closure was extended — details are in our report on cancellations through October 17. Higher energy prices are the other channel: analysts cited in US coverage warned the attacks raise fears of a wider war and more expensive energy, which feeds directly into India's fuel and remittance economics.

What to watch

Three decisions now matter: whether Saudi Arabia launches the large-scale retaliation its coalition has promised, whether Washington moves beyond intelligence support, and whether Turkey takes up Trump's suggestion. Any one of them widens a war that has already reached the departure boards of the Gulf's biggest airport.
